Photograph: Pete Lomchid/Getty Images View image in fullscreen There have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado. Photograph: Pete Lomchid/Getty Images Colorado Sleeping teen and camper wounded as Colorado bear attacks reach record high Bears came through bedroom window and swiped tent at campground, causing scratch marks and puncture wound Uwa Ede-Osifo Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.31 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A black bear burst through a Colorado teenage girl’s window and scratched her, days after a bear also bit a camper in the state, according to wildlife officials. On Friday, a woman at a campground in south-west Colorado heard a growl and felt something hit her outdoors tent, according to a news release. She was treated for a puncture wound on her arm – consistent with a black bear bite – authorities said. Wildlife officers found claw marks on her tent and recovered several dark hairs. “The bite in this incident was more likely an act of surprise than aggression,” said Monte Vista area wildlife manager Rick Basagoitia, adding that the area had “no history of conflict or damage”. Two days later, a bear opened a cracked window, tore the screen off and entered the bedroom of a sleeping 17-year-old girl. The girl was roused by the animal’s presence and hid under her blankets. The bear’s paw struck her stomach, leaving three scratch marks, according to authorities. “The woman is very lucky she had multiple blankets covering her when the bear swiped her,” said district wildlife manager Luke Clancy. There have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado, a number officials have described as unprecedented. A statewide drought has squeezed the food supply of black bears, who mostly eat berries, fruits and insects, officials say. The bears, who seek up to 20,000 calories per day as they prepare to hibernate during the colder months, have sought out new food sources in human residences. Nationwide, there has also been a rise in bear-human conflicts. In August, a bear broke into a New Mexico man’s home and mauled him to death, marking a rare fatal attack for the state. Wildlife officials have urged the public to secure their trash and to lock windows, doors, garages and vehicles. https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: ‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold. Photograph: Claw Films View image in fullscreen ‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold. Photograph: Claw Films Movies ‘Addiction is not only caused by weak will’: how a talking pigeon got Czechia to face up to its alcohol problem Director Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudice Miloš Hroch Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 03.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google C zech film-maker Pepa Lubojacki originally set out to make a film about pigeons. What fascinated the 39-year-old director was that the grey birds are clearly beautiful and highly intelligent creatures, yet human cruelty towards them is socially acceptable in the way it isn’t towards, say, crows or magpies. “You can spot kids kicking and chasing pigeons while their parents cheerfully look on,” she says. The moral blind spot reminded her of the way that people looked at homeless people like her older brother and her cousins. “The public has learned to avert their eyes,” she says. “My cousin was declined care seven times with open wounds in the hospital, and finally, they had to amputate both of his legs.” The birds stayed in the title of her first documentary, one of the most widely discussed and critically lauded films to be released in Czechia in recent years. To make If Pigeons Turned to Gold, Lubojacki spent five years chronicling the lives of four family members on the streets of Prague. In search of answers for why her relatives ended up with addictions and without roofs over their heads, the film wades deep into intergenerational trauma: domestic abuse and the deaths of her biological father and stepfather. Shot mostly on iPhone, the film is narrated by a meme-like talking pigeon and animated family photos with AI voiceovers, including manipulated child portraits of Pepa and her brother. They provide flashbacks to their 90s childhood in prefab estates where “you could get all the drugs your heart desired”, as one of the opening scenes tells us. View image in fullscreen Innovative … the film uses AI to voiceover Pepa and her brother as children. Photograph: Wanda Kaprálová/Claw Films The central focus is Lubojacki’s ever-evasive brother David, and the documentary includes peaceful moments of nostalgic bonding over a rap song, but also documents vicious cycles of alcohol withdrawal and relapse, as Lubojacki struggles to nurture adult David to functionality. It’s an especially pressing issue in Czechia, the home of the world’s most popular beer style in the pilsner, where taxation of alcoholic drinks is traditionally low and the rate of alcohol consumption one of the highest in the world . (To make things worse, Prague has some of the lowest rates of affordable housing in the European Union .) “I was angry because of the systemic injustice,” Lubojacki says. “Police beat up my brother several times, but caring professions can cause violence too, when medical personnel refuse to treat unhoused persons like him because of their history of addiction.” She used to look up to David – a local skater hero who listened to hip-hop, and knew all the cool stuff – and the mission of her film is audiences can “see my brother how I see him and how beautiful he is, that addiction is not only caused by a weak will”. View image in fullscreen Young skater hero … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother David. Photograph: Claw Films If Pigeons Turned to Gold unfolds through diary entries, interspersed with footage of herself on the psychiatric ward where she was hospitalised during the making of the film and video-art sequences of her sinking deep in water. Some of the entries read like poetry: “I’m just a little strawberry seed in the sea, a drowned strawberry seed, in an attempt to change something that is not up to me to change.” “Written text is my primary language and is closer to my heart,” reveals Lubojacki, who also has ambitions as a writer. She was inspired by Ottessa Moshfegh, who writes “simply, almost mechanically, as if without emotions, and observes brutal things without pathos”, and Melissa Broder’s “loose narrative of free writing” on addiction. The central question the 110-minute film circles around is whether you can grieve someone who hasn’t died yet. According to one recent study , people sleeping rough on the streets die 16 years earlier than the rest of the population. “I believe we live in an epidemic of addiction,” Lubojacki says. But speaking about this epidemic without shame is difficult: “When I grew up, I felt isolated, as if I was the only one who had this problem – I couldn’t speak about it with anyone, as I was so ashamed.” View image in fullscreen Pepa Lubojacki with the Berlinale documentary award for If Pigeons Turned to Gold. Photograph: Imago/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News. Relatives of people with addictions often suffer from a secondary trauma, as Barbora Bírová of Czech advocacy organisation Platform for Social Housing points out. “If we understand homelessness as a situation, not as inner personal characteristics, it opens the way to solutions.” Lubojacki had feared rejection, but instead she received acclaim. What began as a student film has already won international recognition on the European film festival circuit. In February, it received the Berlin film festival’s documentary award for “remarkable achievement in recruiting documentary into sustained practice of radical empathy”; at the Karlovy Vary film festival in July, it received a five-minute standing ovation; last month, it was selected as the Czech Republic’s official submission for the 99th Oscars in the International Feature Film category. Hundreds of people have got in touch with Lubojacki to share similar family stories. In her film, pigeons won’t turn to gold or even silver because they are what they are: Lubojacki herself undergoes transformation over the course of the film, from moralising her brother “why don’t you do it for me or mom?” to understanding and acceptance. “Since I understood what was going in his brain, and how I should respond, we have the best relationship we ever had.” The empathy Lubojacki has received gives her hope that people like her brother matter. “We learned to avert our eyes but if one breaks the silence, others will follow.” Explore more on these topics Film Homelessness Czechia Housing Poverty Social exclusion Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
